q-75089.name: Question 1
q-75089.problem:
The matrix $P$ is given below. Let ${p}_{1}$, ${p}_{2}$,  ${p}_{3}$ and ${p}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $P.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(P).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${p}_{4}={x}_{1}{p}_{1}+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}.$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}]
$$
q-75089.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $P$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(P)$ is $\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${p}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{4}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{1}}+{{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 2=4.$

q-75951.name: Question 2
q-75951.problem:
The matrix $Q$ is given below. Let ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$, and ${q}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $Q.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${q}_{3}={x}_{1}{q}_{1}+{x}_{2}{q}_{2}.$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$
q-75951.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{1}}+{{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 2=4.$

[28]⏟q3=(2)⏟x1⋅[12]⏟q1+(2)⏟x2⋅[02]⏟q2.

q-75980.name: Question 3
q-75980.problem:
The matrix $V$ is given below. Let ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2}$,  ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $V.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{v}_{1},{v}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${v}_{2}={x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}.$ 

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$
q-75980.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $V$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{10}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(V)$ is $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}\}.$ 

Therefore, we conclude that $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{3}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$

q-75982.name: Question 4
q-75982.problem:
The matrix $F$ is given below. Let ${f}_{1}$, ${f}_{2}$,  ${f}_{3}$ and ${f}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $F.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{f}_{1},{f}_{2},{f}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(F).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${f}_{4}={x}_{1}{f}_{1}+{x}_{2}{f}_{2}+{x}_{3}{f}_{3}.$ 

$$
F=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -4 & -24 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -6 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$
q-75982.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $F$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -4 & -24 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -6 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -6 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(F)$ is $\{{f}_{1},{f}_{2}\}.$ 

Therefore, we conclude that $B=\{{f}_{1},{f}_{2},{f}_{3}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(F).$

Determine if $B=\text{{}{h}_{1},{h}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(H).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${h}_{2}={x}_{1}{h}_{1}+{x}_{3}{h}_{3}.$

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & -8 \\ -3 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$
q-111504.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $H$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}H & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & -8 \\ -3 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ -3 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(H)$ is $\{{h}_{1},{h}_{2}\}.$

Therefore, we conclude that $\text{{}{h}_{1},{h}_{3}\text{}}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(H).$
